title: Seoul expands tick surveillance to prevent infection surge during autumn - The Korea Times

analysis.time: Seoul is expanding tick surveillance as autumn approaches, following the first SFTS death of the year on Jeju Island on August 28, 2026. The surveillance runs from April through October, with data collected through August.
analysis.location_and_population: The Seoul Research Institute of Public Health and Environment is monitoring high-risk green spaces such as Han River parks, ecological reserves, hiking paths, barefoot walking zones, and dog parks. Outdoor animals, including stray cats and shelter pets, are also being tested.
analysis.event: Seoul has expanded tick surveillance in parks and walking trails to prevent an infection surge during autumn, following the first SFTS death of the year on Jeju Island. The surveillance includes testing ticks and animals for the SFTS virus.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of August, approximately 480 ticks have been collected with no SFTS virus detected. Of 108 animals tested between April and late July, none tested positive. SFTS has a fatality rate of 12 to 30 percent due to the lack of targeted antiviral treatments or vaccines.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Seoul Research Institute of Public Health and Environment is conducting intensive monitoring and testing. Health officials urge the public to use repellents, wear long sleeves, and check for ticks after outdoor activities. The agency also conducts annual animal surveillance tests to track potential viral reservoirs.

analysis.brief_en: Seoul is expanding tick surveillance in parks and walking trails as autumn approaches, following the first Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) death of the year on Jeju Island on August 28, 2026. The Seoul Research Institute of Public Health and Environment is monitoring high-risk green spaces, including Han River parks, ecological reserves, hiking paths, barefoot walking zones, and dog parks, from April through October. As of August, 480 ticks have been collected with no SFTS virus detected, and 108 animals tested between April and late July showed no positives. SFTS, transmitted by infected hard ticks like the Asian bush tick, has a fatality rate of 12 to 30 percent due to the absence of targeted treatments or vaccines. Health officials advise using repellents, wearing long sleeves, and checking for ticks after outdoor activities. The agency also conducts annual animal surveillance tests to monitor potential viral reservoirs.
analysis.summary_en: Seoul is expanding tick surveillance in parks and walking trails as autumn approaches, following the first Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) death of the year on Jeju Island on August 28, 2026. The Seoul Research Institute of Public Health and Environment is monitoring high-risk green spaces, including Han River parks, ecological reserves, hiking paths, barefoot walking zones, and dog parks, from April through October. As of August, 480 ticks have been collected with no SFTS virus detected, and 108 animals tested between April and late July showed no positives. SFTS, transmitted by infected hard ticks like the Asian bush tick, has a fatality rate of 12 to 30 percent due to the absence of targeted treatments or vaccines. Health officials advise using repellents, wearing long sleeves, and checking for ticks after outdoor activities. The agency also conducts annual animal surveillance tests to monitor potential viral reservoirs.
